messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Chaplain
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Crowding: Crowded places, Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Somchai was a 34-year-old South Eastern Asian man who had come to the clinic after months of feeling unable to settle back into his life as a chaplain. He had been widowed before the assault, and since then he had carried a solemn, restrained manner that made it easy for others to assume he was composed. In the months after the mugging, however, he found that composure slipping in ways he could not control. The attack had happened late in the evening as he was walking home alone after visiting a parishioner. A man and another person he later understood to be connected with the robbery closed in quickly, demanding his wallet and phone. In the confusion, Somchai became acutely aware of the closeness of their bodies, the urgency in their breathing, and the sense that there was nowhere to step aside. What stayed with him most was not a clear narrative but flashes: a sudden movement toward him, the glint of a hand, the narrow street, the sensation that the whole scene had happened faster than he could take in. Even now, when he tried to describe it, he spoke in images rather than in sequence, as if the memory arrived as separate pictures he could not arrange into a coherent story.

He had also noticed that the memory came with smells. At unexpected moments he would catch an odor that seemed to belong to that night, and the combination of the image and the smell would bring him straight back into the alley in a way that felt immediate and humiliating. When that happened, the memory did not feel like something distant he could reflect on safely; it felt present, invasive, and raw. He said that what often returned was not only fear but a sharp wave of rage. He would remember the men closing in, remember the helplessness of having to hand over what they wanted, and feel furious all over again at the violation of it. He disliked that intensity because it seemed to clash with the role he had always tried to inhabit, yet the anger arrived forcefully whenever the event came back to him.

Over time, several ordinary situations began to feel loaded with danger. Crowded places were especially difficult. In supermarkets, in church hallways after services, and on public sidewalks during community events, he found himself scanning for ways people might come too close. The press of bodies, the lack of open space, and the sense of being hemmed in brought back the evening of the robbery so vividly that he would tense and hurry through rather than linger. As a chaplain, he could not avoid people altogether, but he began making subtle changes to his routines. He accepted fewer evening visits and chose routes that felt easier to move through. At work, he became increasingly uneasy when he was around people whose behavior reminded him of those connected to the event, not because they were exactly the same, but because they seemed to belong to that same category in his mind of people who might suddenly turn threatening. He did not trust his own ability to read them quickly enough, and that uncertainty made him cautious in ways others did not always notice.

The sound that most reliably unsettled him was heavy breathing. If someone nearby was breathing loudly, especially in a confined space or in a crowd, Somchai would feel his attention lock onto it. The sound seemed to carry him back to the robbery, to the closeness and urgency of the attackers, and he would become watchful, waiting for the next movement he feared might follow. He described these moments as intensely uncomfortable and said he could not simply ignore them. He would try to focus on prayer or conversation, but his attention would keep returning to the breath, the noise, the immediate sense that something bad was about to happen.

As the months passed, Somchai increasingly came to believe that the attack fit some flaw in him rather than something random. He was convinced that the event happened to him because of the sort of person he was. He spoke with visible distress about how someone else would not have gotten into that situation, as if other people possessed a kind of instinct or strength that he lacked. He could not shake the thought that he had been too trusting, too open, or too exposed, though he did not frame this as an abstract idea so much as a personal failing that made the robbery feel deserved in a distorted, painful way. Alongside that, he found himself thinking that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. The certainty was stark and discouraging: if it had happened once, it could happen again, and his own caution seemed inadequate against that possibility.

By the time he sought help, the strain was showing in both his personal and professional life. He felt ashamed that, as a chaplain, he was expected to be steady for others while privately feeling cornered by memories and triggers that could be set off by a crowded parish event or the wrong sound in a hallway. What finally brought him in was the fear that he was becoming smaller and more restricted without meaning to, and that his world would keep narrowing if he did not ask for support. He said he wanted to be able to move through crowds, hear a person breathe heavily, or think back on the robbery without being thrown so completely back into it. At the same time, he was afraid that the event had changed him in a permanent way and that he would never again feel fully safe in the ordinary places where his life now had to happen.
